paper_title: Hierarchical Residuals: A Minimalist Decoupling of Residual Width from Compute Width

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Residual connections underpin Transformers, but they implicitly tie the residual width carried through depth to the compute width used inside each layer. We introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), a minimalist architectural change that decouples these dimensions, widening the residual state while keeping per-layer compute width fixed. HiRes groups layers into blocks: standard d-dimensional PreNorm layers operate inside each block, while a wider D-dimensional PostNorm outer residual connects blocks. Learned read/write projections bridge the two spaces at block boundaries, leaving individual Transformer layers unchanged. Across different model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition, with fitted scaling laws indicating a 1.30-fold improvement in FLOPs efficiency. On OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining for 500B tokens, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. HiRes is also competitive with other residual expansion methods such as VWN, mHC and AttnRes with less activation memory and I/O costs. Built from only dense projections and normalizations, it requires neither specialized kernels nor infrastructure-level optimizations. HiRes thus exposes residual width as a practical scaling variable using only standard operators.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Residual connections [14] are the backbone of modern Transformers. standard PreNorm layer reads from normalized copy of the current hidden state, computes an update, and adds that back to the original state [47, 54]. Repeating this operation yields simple yet effective transport rule: one d-dimensional state is carried through depth along an identity path, while every attention and feed-forward module contributes an additive update. This design makes deep optimization practical, but it also ties the width of the state carried through depth to the width of the working space of every layer. Recent residual architectures relax this constraint in different ways. Alternating Updates (AltUp) maintains multiple residual streams, with each layer computing one stream and predicting the remainder [4]. HyperConnections (HC) likewise uses multiple streams but learns how layers read from, write to, and combine them with lightweight projectors [59]; Virtual Width Networks (VWN) generalizes this formulation by splitting each stream into finer granularity [38]; Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) stabilizes HC by constraining its residual mixing operators to doubly stochastic manifold [53]. Attention Residuals instead retrieves representations from earlier layers using attention over depth [20]. Gray and navy paths have width and D; orange trapezoids are the added dense interfaces, and dashed frames mark repeated residual units. residual operators with different update rules. Nevertheless, they share two recurring departures from vanilla residual addition: (i) the effective residual state is expanded, and (ii) residual accumulation becomes explicitly regulated, keeping the residual scale in check. This suggests that residual-state capacity is an architectural variable in its own right, rather than quantity that must always equal model width. However, their per-layer expanded states and intricate mixing add activation traffic and memory-bound residual operators, typically requiring fusion, recomputation, overlap, or specialized kernels to recover throughput [53]. If the benefit stems from the wider state itself rather than particular operators, natural question arises: can Transformers benefit from wider residual state with as little architectural change as possible? To this end, we introduce Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes). HiRes groups adjacent Transformer layers into layer blocks and organizes residual computation at two levels. Inside each block, the model runs ordinary d-dimensional PreNorm Transformer layers. Across blocks, it maintains D-dimensional outer residual state with the familiar additive update (D > d). read projection maps the outer state into block, and after the inner residual accumulation, write projection maps the resulting inner state back. The block write is added to the outer residual and the sum is then post-normalized, which regulates the residual scale. Thus, the outer recurrence retains the familiar PostNorm residual, while the inner Transformer layers are unchanged. In this way, the residual expansion ratio D/d can be selected independently of the compute width for each inner layer. Because read/write operations occur only at block boundaries, the additional parameters and compute costs are amortized over depth. Figure 1 places the two levels side by side: the outer recurrence is the residual motif of vanilla PostNorm Transformer, with whole layer block in place of sublayer. Empirically, HiRes consistently outperforms vanilla residual addition across model sizes and depths. Under fitted loss-compute scaling laws, it is 1.30 more FLOP-efficient. As depth scales up at fixed width, HiRes continues to improve through 128 layers where the baseline exhibits diminishing returns. Against HyperConnections, mHC, VWN, and Attention Residuals, HiRes remains comparable in quality at lower activation memory and I/O costs. On OLMoE-1B-7B [30] pretraining for 500B tokens (Section 3.5), HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 1.14-point higher downstream accuracy. Overall, HiRes provides minimalist way to expand the residual state without widening per-layer compute. It shows that decoupling residual width from compute width is beneficial, and that this decoupling is available with standard operators.

sections.title: 2.4 Design Choices
sections.content: Normalization at block boundaries. Boundary normalization provides residual regulation in HiRes: without it, the outer residual stream would be unbounded as it accumulates block outputs. Keeping PreNorm within blocks and applying PostNorm between them combines PreNorms optimization stability during the backward pass [50, 54] with PostNorms periodic control of the outer residual scale during the forward pass [19]. Setting = and Rb = Wb = in Equation (4) and removing the outer residual accumulation yields hierarchical normalization (HiNorm): xb+1,0 = RMSNormb(Φb(xb,0)), = 1, . . . , B, (6) which inserts one RMSNorm into the residual stream every L/B layers. HiNorm isolates regulation from residual expansion and serves as control in our experiments. HiNorm alone beats the baseline and reaches minimum loss at an intermediate = 4 (Appendix Figure 6a). In Appendix Figure 6b, the residual scale grows monotonically in the vanilla baseline and in HiRes without boundary normalization. HC, VWN, and AttnRes [20, 38, 59] regulate the scale implicitly through residual mixing learned at every layer, whereas HiRes regulates it explicitly with boundary normalizations: the scale grows only within each block and is reset at every boundary. Interface stabilization. We empirically observe that randomly initialized interfaces degrade performance early in training (Appendix D.2.2), which we hypothesize arises from seesaw dynamic: the interfaces learn each blocks working coordinate system while the inner layers simultaneously learn to transform representations within that evolving space. sections.title: 3.1 Setup
sections.content: We conduct the primary architecture study using the OLMoE codebase [30]. All models use RMSNorm [56], RoPE [44], grouped-query attention (GQA) [1], and SwiGLU feed-forward network [39]. We train with AdamW [24] and cosine learning-rate schedule with warmup, use 4096-token context, and initialize weights with standard deviation 0.02. The default HiRes configuration uses residual expansion ratio = D/d = 2 and block count = 4. We ablate both choices in Section 4.1. For architecture comparisons, we average training loss over the final 1000 steps. Validation loss and downstream accuracy are averaged over the final 3 evaluations, 1000 steps apart, and across 11 held-out domains and 12 tasks, respectively. sections.content: We next examine depth scaling properties of HiRes by fixing the inner width at = 512 and the training budget at 30B tokens while increasing the number of Transformer layers from 8 to 128. Figure 3 plots validation loss against depth on logarithmic axis, where ideal compute scaling should appear as straight line. HiRes not only consistently outperforms the vanilla residual baseline at every depth, but also maintains better scaling properties. The baseline bends away from its scaling curve at the last doubling from = 64 to = 128. With = 4, HiRes gives up less of its per-doubling reduction than the baseline, especially at = 2, indicating that regulating residual accumulation and widening the residual state can hold more layers. sections.title: 3.5 Long-Horizon MoE Pretraining
sections.content: To scale up, we evaluate HiRes on the OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining recipe [30], sparse Mixture-of-Experts model [12, 40]. The model contains 6.9B total parameters and 1.3B active parameters per token, and is trained for 500B tokens. We compare the vanilla residual baseline with HiRes using the = 2, = 4 configuration, which adds 83.9M parameters (6.5% of the active parameters and 1.2% of the total parameters); Appendix Table 9 lists the full configuration. As shown in Figure 4, HiRes achieves 0.0208 lower training loss and 0.0180 lower validation loss than the vanilla residual baseline. It also performs better on most downstream tasks and improves the downstream average accuracy by 1.14 points. These results establish that the HiRes design transfers to long-horizon sparse-MoE pretraining. Figure 4 HiRes on 500B-token OLMoE-1B-7B pretraining. sections.title: 4.1 Ablation on Block Count and Expansion Ratio
sections.content: We ablate the two structural hyperparameters of HiRes: the residual expansion ratio and the number of blocks B. All runs use (d, L) = (768, 12) and 50B training tokens. The expansion sweep fixes = 4 and varies = D/d from 0.75 to 4, while the block sweep fixes = 2 and varies from 1 to 12. Figure 5 reports both sweeps. Expansion ratio. In Figure 5a, validation loss rapidly decreases as the expansion ratio increases to = 2, after which the slope slows. The wider = 3 and = 4 settings provide marginal gains, largely following the shifted scaling law, which accounts for the benefit from extra parameters. Thus = 2 is the empirical knee of the quality-overhead curve: it captures most of the benefit of residual expansion while keeping the interface cost moderate. On the other side, at = 0.75 the outer state is narrower than the layer compute width, and it is the only point in the sweep that fails to improve over HiNorm, even with more parameters. This result identifies residual width, rather than the interfaces themselves, as the main source of the gain. Number of blocks. In Figure 5b, increasing also improves validation loss, with the largest gains occurring as the hierarchy is refined from one to four blocks. Beyond = 4, more frequent outer-state updates show diminishing returns similar to those of the expansion ratio. We therefore retain = 4 as the empirical knee.

sections.title:
5 Related Work
Residual-state expansion. The closest methods expand the residual state, but typically by replacing vanilla
addition with a learned, per-layer operator. AltUp widens the representation into sub-blocks and updates
one sub-block at backbone width while a lightweight predictor updates the rest [4]. Hyper-Connections
(HC) maintains multiple residual streams with learned layer-dependent read, write, and residual mixing
weights [59]; Virtual Width Networks (VWN) generalizes HC by constructing fine-grained fractional streams,
enabling more expressive mixing [38, 60]; mHC constrains the residual stream transition to a doubly stochastic
manifold for stability [53]. Attention Residuals instead learns content-dependent attention over earlier layer
or block representations [20]. Relative to this family, HiRes is simpler in mechanism: one wide outer state,
dense read/write only at block boundaries, and additive residual transport. It maintains more expressive
interfaces between the expanded residual and the fixed-width inner state, and amortizes the cost across depth.
sections.content: Normalization in Transformers. The original Transformer normalizes after each residual addition (PostNorm), whereas modern language models typically use PreNorm to keep an uninterrupted additive path through depth [2, 31, 47, 54, 56]. There exists well-known trade-off between PreNorm and PostNorm: PostNorm controls activation scale but can attenuate gradients, while PreNorm eases optimization but lets the residual state grow unbounded [49]. Hybrid placements pursue both, adding normalization inside the residual branches [41], around each sublayer [19], mixed within sublayer [61], across depth [21], or across coupled PreNorm-like and PostNorm-like streams [22]. HiRes differs in granularity: complete PreNorm layers run inside block, and PostNorm is applied only after the block-level outer residual addition, preserving ordinary inner updates while periodically resetting the outer-state scale. Cross-layer connectivity and state aggregation. Prior work enriches information flow across depth through gated shortcuts, identity paths, or dense connectivity [14, 17, 43]. Transformer variants further aggregate earlier representations using static weights, element-wise gates, reused values, or low-rank projections [11, 26, 32, 58], while MUDDFormer mixes decoupled streams and Deep Delta Learning maintains matrix-valued state [52, 57]. HiRes instead uses hierarchical connectivity, combining persistent wide outer state across blocks with narrow inner states within each block.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced Hierarchical Residuals (HiRes), deliberately minimal architecture that decouples residualstate width from per-layer compute width. HiRes carries wide persistent state across layer blocks, performs ordinary Transformer computation in narrower inner space, and connects the two through learned read/write projections at block boundaries. This hierarchical design uses only dense linear maps, normalization, and residual addition, requiring neither specialized kernels nor changes to the inner Transformer layers. Across model sizes and depths, HiRes consistently outperforms the vanilla residual baseline and is competitive with other residual expansion methods including HC, VWN, mHC, and AttnRes. These results demonstrate that residual-state width need not be tied to per-layer compute width and that their conventional equality can be suboptimal. HiRes therefore establishes residual width as practical scaling variable that can be exploited through simple yet effective hierarchical design.

sections.title: A Implementation Pseudocode
sections.content: HiRes can be implemented as simple extension of vanilla Transformer by changing fewer than ten lines of code in the models forward method, as illustrated in Algorithm 1. Algorithm 1 PyTorch-style pseudocode of the HiRes forward pass. def forward(self, input_ids): = self.embed(input_ids) x_outer = self.embed_proj(x) # up-project -> for in range(self.num_blocks): # Read at block entry, down-project -> x_inner = self.read_proj[b](x_outer) # Standard PreNorm inner residual for in range(self.num_layers // self.num_blocks): x_inner = x_inner + self.attn[b][i](self.attn_norm[b][i](x_inner)) x_inner = x_inner + self.ffn[b][i](self.ffn_norm[b][i](x_inner)) # Write at block exit, up-project -> x_outer = self.outer_norm[b](x_outer + self.write_proj[b](x_inner)) = self.lm_head_proj(x_outer) # down-project -> logits = self.lm_head(self.final_layernorm(x)) return logits

sections.title: B Experimental Setup
sections.content: All dense experiments use decoder-only Transformers implemented in the OLMoE codebase [30]. Models use weight-tied input/output embeddings, RMSNorm [56], RoPE [44], SwiGLU [39] with preactivation width dff = 4d, grouped-query attention [1] with head dimension 64 and 4 KV heads, and per-head QK-norm [9]. 8, weight decay 0.1, and gradient-norm clipping Training uses AdamW [24] with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.95, ϵ = 10 at 1.0. The learning rate uses cosine decay to 0.1 of the peak rate after linear warmup over 2% of training tokens. Models use 4,096-token sequence length and initialization standard deviation 0.02. Table 4 lists the scale-dependent settings. The training corpus is the OLMo2 stage-1 mixture, tokenized with the Dolma2 tokenizer and its 100,352token vocabulary [48]. All compared architectures at given scale reuse the same data order and global sample-index array. Validation loss is averaged over 11 held-out domains from Paloma [25]: C4 [33], Dolma Books, Dolma Common Crawl, Dolma Pes2o, Dolma Reddit, Dolma Stack, Dolma Wiki [42], ICE, M2D2 S2ORC [23, 34], Pile [13], and WikiText-103 [27]. Downstream accuracy is averaged over 12 tasks: MMLU [15], ARC-Challenge and ARC-Easy [7], BoolQ [6], CommonsenseQA [45], COPA [35], HellaSwag [55], OpenBookQA [28], PIQA [5], SciQ [51], SocialIQA [37], and WinoGrande [36]. sections.title: G A Latent View
sections.content: Besides expanding the residual state width, HiRes also admits dual interpretation: relative to Ddimensional persistent hidden state, its attention and FFN computation occurs in d-dimensional latent space. Expanding residual width by = D/d is therefore equivalent to compressing compute width by factor of n; the wide state preserves information across blocks, while the narrow state performs the transformations within each block. This view connects HiRes to module-specific latent designs. MLA compresses the attention KV representation [8], while LatentMoE performs routed expert computation in compressed space [10]. HiRes extends the same separation between state width and compute width to the residual hierarchy. Its key distinction is interaction granularity: instead of exchanging information between hidden and latent spaces at every sublayer, HiRes reads once at block entry and writes once at block exit. Layer grouping therefore reduces hidden-latent transport from per-sublayer to per-block while allowing computation to evolve for multiple layers in the latent space.

sections.title: H Limitations
sections.content: Our study has the following limitations. First, HiRes decouples residual width from compute width, but we have not jointly optimized these widths and model depth under fixed compute budget. The best allocation of capacity between carrying representations and transforming them therefore remains unclear. Second, we use equal-sized blocks, so exchanges between the wide state and the inner computation occur at regular intervals. We have not examined whether different parts of the network benefit from more frequent access to the wide state. Finally, our results show the benefits of residual expansion, yet how the wider residual state improves learning remains an open question. In particular, what information is preserved across blocks and how individual sublayers contribute to its transformation and reuse are not yet well understood.
